subject: Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution

messages.author: fde4048c840328bf
messages.subject: Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution
parts:
Hi all,

I am just curious about one thing. Let us consider the example in page 105 of the Manual (Stochastic Volatility). When using standard Gibbs Sampler methods, we can filter the stochastic volatility either using a Kalman Filter (doing an approximation to a mixture of Normal distributions first) or using direct non-linear methods like the Particle Filter. In general, if we use these methods, we have the "Filtering" distribution, which is used to evaluate likelihood functions or to do model diagnostics, and the "Smoothing" distribution, which is more suitable when the objective is to analyze the true evolution of the volatility over time (since it uses all the information in the sample). I am just wondering how the estimated path for volatility that we will get in STAN from the example will relate to those two distributions...

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution
parts:
To get the approximation, you code up the approximation
in Stan directly. To get samples from the true posterior, just use
the model. You basically get draws for the parameters of the
log probability function you define conditioned on the given data
(i.e., most commonly a Bayesian posterior in Stan applications, but
you can sample from any density you can write down a log probability
function for up to a constant).

My understanding is that a Kalman filter implies a particular form
of model (and I tend to think of them as synonymous with the model
structure, not the algorithm for fitting them by Kalman):

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter#Underlying_dynamic_system_model

whereas a particle filter is a very algorithm for estimation:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_filter

The whole literature's confusing because particle filters are
often used synonymously with the particular time-series
model they're estimating.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution
parts:
Bob,

Thank you very much for your reply. I understand that, but maybe I am just overthinking too much or I did not explain myself properly. Just to simplify, in the code from the example, we will get a posterior distribution for the distribution of h, at each period of time. Then, if I compute the quantiles at each time period t, I can see an "estimated" median path for a time series that represents the movement of volatility over time. My question is if we can rely on this path to be a representation/estimation of the true path for volatility.

I am asking this because when we use the Kalman Filter or the Particle Filter to estimate that time series path, Chris Sims claims that the filter will show time variation in the state variable (in this case, volatility), even if the true data generating process has no time variation at all. And this is why we use the "Smoother" after passing the filter when we use standard Gibbs methods (also called the FFBS algorithm), which in principle, should show a better approximation of the true evolution of volatility in the data generating process. 

The idea is that the filter gives at each time period t only the distribution of the volatility at time t conditional on the information up to time t, but the smoothing gives the distribution of volatility at time t, conditional on the information in the full sample (1 to T). So, I am just a bit worried that I might have the same problem with the output from STAN... My guess is that it is not a problem since the code in the example considers each volatility at period t a parameter in the model, and the estimation of the model considers the likelihood of the full sample, but I am not sure.

Having said that, I have done a considerable amount of Monte Carlo experiments, and STAN seems to work fine. That is, it usually captures the true movement of volatility over time. But I am just concerned about the theoretical properties...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution
parts:
On 11/19/13, 1:56 PM, Carlos wrote:
> Bob,
>
> Thank you very much for your reply. I understand that, but maybe I am just overthinking too much or I did not explain
> myself properly. Just to simplify, in the code from the example, we will get a posterior distribution for the
> distribution of h, at each period of time. Then, if I compute the quantiles at each time period t, I can see an
> "estimated" median path for a time series that represents the movement of volatility over time. My question is if we can
> rely on this path to be a representation/estimation of the true path for volatility.

That median's an MCMC estimate of the true median of the posterior.
Now whether that represents the truth is a modeling question, and
I don't know much about computational finance or econometrics.

In the Bayesian approach, you'd just add a parameter for
that latent true value and look at the distribution of that.

> I am asking this because when we use the Kalman Filter or the Particle Filter to estimate that time series path, Chris
> Sims claims that the filter will show time variation in the state variable (in this case, volatility), even if the true
> data generating process has no time variation at all.

That may be true. But will the estimates be in the 95%
interval 95% of the time? In this case, if the true variation
is 0, does the 95% posterior interval (the quantiles of the
posterior samples) contain the value 0 roughly 95% of the time.

You can just use simulation to measure this. In fact,
we recommend people do this kind of simulated data fitting
for any model that they look at (we do it for our own models).

> And this is why we use the "Smoother" after passing the filter
> when we use standard Gibbs methods (also called the FFBS algorithm), which in principle, should show a better
> approximation of the true evolution of volatility in the data generating process.

A smoother is just going to act like a prior in a Bayesian model
or a regularizer in a penalized maximum likelihood model. You can
put that kind of smoothing in the model, but the estimate should
be your estimate. The trick of the Bayesian approach is to keep
the uncertainty of your estimate in mind.

> The idea is that the filter gives at each time period t only the distribution of the volatility at time t conditional on
> the information up to time t, but the smoothing gives the distribution of volatility at time t, conditional on the
> information in the full sample (1 to T). So, I am just a bit worried that I might have the same problem with the output
> from STAN... My guess is that it is not a problem since the code in the example considers each volatility at period t a
> parameter in the model, and the estimation of the model considers the likelihood of the full sample, but I am not sure.

This question's really independent of Stan. Stan just
defines a probability function p(theta,y) where theta is
a sequence of parameters and y is data and then draws
samples from p(theta|y), which is proportional to p(theta,y).

> Having said that, I have done a considerable amount of Monte Carlo experiments, and STAN seems to work fine. That is, it
> usually captures the true movement of volatility over time. But I am just concerned about the theoretical properties...

The theoretical properties of Stan are the usual ones for
MCMC. We have some people on this list who know that much
better than me.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Example - Question about the distribution
parts:
Just to follow up/reinforce a few points.

Firstly, the output from Stan is equivalent to the smoothed estimate - you're building a joint model of all of the points at once. You can use the Stan output to estimate a new time, which would be equivalent to a new filtering update, modulo the incorporation of uncertainty.

By the way, the false volatility arises because you're trying to make an extrapolation without shrinking back to the mean, which is why smoothing (or fitting all the time points at once) removes this effect.

Additionally, do not interpret the median at each time as an actual path! This is true for a smoothed estimate or a Bayesian estimate. The most likely path is very different from the marginally most likely points at given times.
